The church did not usually forbid women to doubt with a rule. We did something quieter and more effective. We made it socially costly, and then we called the resulting silence peace.

The cost of that silence was not only to the women. A church that only hears its men's questions is a church half-thinking, missing the interrogation of exactly the readers who most needed the faith to be true, the mothers holding grief, the daughters reading the hard texts about their own place. When we silenced the women's doubts, we did not protect the faith. We amputated part of the church's capacity to think, and we told the amputees it was for their own good.

## To the woman doubting in the dark

So let me say directly to the woman who has been carrying questions she has never been allowed to speak. Your doubt is not a betrayal of your faith. It may be the most faithful thing about you, because it means you refuse to pretend, and God has never once asked you to pretend. He put Job's rage in the Bible. He put the psalmist's abandonment in the Bible. He answered "help my unbelief" with healing and not with a lecture. The God you are questioning is not fragile, and he is not offended by your honesty. He is far more grieved by the pious performance that hides the ache than by the ache itself.

You were not put here to be the emotional caretaker of everyone else's faith while your own goes unexamined and unfed. You are a thinking, questioning image-bearer of God, and your questions belong in the church, spoken out loud, taken seriously, sat with by people who will not rush to resolve them because they are afraid of them. The church that could not hold your doubt was too small. It was not your faith that failed. It was our courage.

Keep the question inside the faith rather than leaving to keep it. The doubt is not the door out. It can be the way in, because a God who is true has nothing to fear from an honest question, and the church that finally learns this will discover it was the doubters, all along, who were taking God the most seriously. They were the ones who refused to lie about him. That was never the weak faith. We only called it that because it frightened us.

chapters.title: Women and Leadership in the Church
chapters.summary: The women were already leading in Acts. The question of women and church leadership is older and more open than the certainties on either side pretend, and the deeper problem is what we think leadership is.
chapters.body:
I want to take up the question of women and leadership in the church directly, and I want to do it without the confidence that usually accompanies it. On this subject the loudest voices are the surest ones, and I have come to distrust the correlation between volume and truth. Let me start with what is not actually in dispute, because a great deal is not, and then move to what is, and then to the thing underneath both that I think we have missed.

## What is not in dispute

It is not in dispute that women led in the earliest church. I do not mean this as an argument for any particular position. I mean it as a fact of the text that both sides have to account for. Phoebe was a diakonos, a deacon, of the church at Cenchreae, and the courier of the letter to the Romans (Romans 16:1 to 2). Priscilla taught Apollos (Acts 18:26). Junia was, in Paul's words, "well known among the apostles" (Romans 16:7). The four daughters of Philip the evangelist "prophesied" (Acts 21:9). Women prayed and prophesied in the Corinthian assembly, which is why Paul gives instructions about how, not whether, they should do it (1 Corinthians 11:5). The prophecy Peter quotes at Pentecost is explicit: "your sons and your daughters shall prophesy" (Acts 2:17).

Whatever a church concludes about the office of elder, it has to reckon with the plain fact that women in the New Testament taught, prophesied, served as deacons, hosted churches in their homes, funded the mission, and carried the theology. The image of the early church as a male institution with women in the pews is not a picture the New Testament supports. It is a picture we painted later.

Consider how many of the first churches met in homes owned or hosted by women. There was Lydia, the dealer in purple goods, in whose house the church at Philippi first gathered (Acts 16:15, 16:40). There was Nympha, in whose house a church met in Colossae (Colossians 4:15). There was Mary the mother of John Mark, whose home in Jerusalem was a gathering place for prayer (Acts 12:12). In a world where hosting the assembly meant a measure of oversight and provision and standing within it, the record keeps naming women as the ones who held that place. None of this settles the question of the ordained office. But it means that any honest account of leadership in the earliest church has to begin by admitting how much of the load women were already carrying, in public, with the church's blessing and Luke's plain approval.

## What is in dispute

What is in dispute is narrower than the volume of the argument suggests. It is the question of the ordained office of elder or pastor, and whether the New Testament restricts it to qualified men. Two texts carry most of the weight. In 1 Corinthians 14:34 Paul writes that "the women should keep silent in the churches." In 1 Timothy 2:12 he writes, "I do not permit a woman to teach or to exercise authority over a man; rather, she is to remain quiet."

The complementarian reads these as normative and permanent, grounded, in the 1 Timothy case, in the order of creation rather than in local circumstance, since Paul immediately appeals to "For Adam was formed first, then Eve" (1 Timothy 2:13). That is the strongest card in the complementarian hand and I will not pretend it is weak. It is not a cultural argument. It reaches back before the fall.

The egalitarian reads these texts as bound to their occasions. The Corinthian silence, she notes, sits three chapters after Paul assumed women were prophesying aloud in the same assembly, which means "keep silent" cannot be absolute or Paul contradicts himself within one letter, so it must address a specific disorder. The Ephesian prohibition, she argues, addresses a specific crisis of false teaching in that city, in which women appear to have been particular targets and carriers of the error, and the appeal to Adam and Eve answers a specific false teaching about creation rather than legislating for all time. New Testament scholars like Gordon Fee and Craig Keener have made this case carefully, and it is not a case built on ignoring the text but on reading it in its situation.

## The order of the question, again

I said it in another place and I will say it here because it governs everything: this is a second-order question. The creeds do not settle it. Chalcedon does not settle it. Faithful, Bible-believing, gospel-preaching churches have landed on both sides for centuries and remained the church. That fact should make all of us slower and gentler than we tend to be. When a complementarian speaks of an egalitarian church as though it had denied the faith, or an egalitarian speaks of a complementarian church as though it were merely bigotry in a collar, both have made a second-order question do first-order work, and both are wrong to.

I hold a view. I lean toward the fuller participation of women, including in teaching and, in my reading, in the eldership, for reasons drawn from the whole sweep of Scripture and the clear leadership of women within it. And the strongest objection to my view, which I have not fully dissolved, remains that appeal to creation in 1 Timothy 2:13, which does not read like a cultural aside. An honest man holds his position with that unanswered pressure in view and does not pretend the other side is composed of fools. It is not.

## The thing underneath

But I said there was something underneath both positions, and this is what I most want you to hear. The entire debate assumes we already know what church leadership is, and I am no longer sure we do.

We argue about who gets to lead as though leadership were a possession, a status, a platform, an authority to be distributed. And every time the New Testament touches the subject of leadership among God's people, it does something disorienting. It refuses to define leadership as status and redefines it as service, to the point of reversal. "You know that those who are considered rulers of the Gentiles lord it over them, and their great ones exercise authority over them. But it shall not be so among you. But whoever would be great among you must be your servant" (Mark 10:42 to 43). Jesus, the night before he died, took off his outer garment, wrapped a towel around his waist, and washed his disciples' feet, the task of the lowest slave in the house, and then said, "I have given you an example, that you also should do just as I have done to you" (John 13:15).

The disciples spent that entire evening arguing about who was the greatest. It is almost comic. On the night of the foot washing, at the Last Supper itself, Luke tells us "a dispute also arose among them, as to which of them was to be regarded as the greatest" (Luke 22:24). They could not stop competing for the top even as the Lord knelt at their feet demonstrating that the top was the bottom. And I read that scene and I recognize the whole church, complementarian and egalitarian alike, arguing over who gets the authority while the basin sits unused in the corner.

Lesslie Newbigin, the missionary theologian who spent decades in India before returning to a secularized Britain he no longer recognized, argued that the church's fundamental problem in the modern West was that it had absorbed the culture's account of power and freedom without noticing, so that even its internal debates were being fought on terms borrowed from the world rather than from the gospel. I think that diagnosis lands directly on the leadership question. We have, most of us, an account of leadership drawn from the corporation, the campaign, and the platform, an account in which leadership means visibility, influence, and the authority to direct others. And then we open the New Testament, which defines leadership as the willingness to be the servant and the slave of all, and we quietly keep the corporate definition while arguing about who may hold the corporate office. The debate feels biblical because it uses biblical texts. But the underlying picture of what a leader is has often been imported whole from a world that has never washed a foot in its life.

## What I learned from having no one to imitate

I did not grow up with a father, which means I did not grow up watching a man lead a home, and when I became a pastor I had no inherited model of what spiritual authority looked like up close. I had to build it from the text and from failure. And the thing I built, slowly, is a conviction that has quietly reordered how I read this whole debate.

The authority that actually forms people is not the authority that is granted by an office. I have known men with the office of elder who could not lead a family out of a burning building, and I have known women with no office at all whose spiritual authority in my congregation was undeniable, unappointed, and real, women whose counsel elders sought, whose prayers moved things, whose presence made a room more honest. The Spirit had granted them an authority no committee had voted on. And I began to suspect that the church's obsession with who may hold the office had blinded us to who actually carries the weight, which is often not the same set of people.

This does not resolve the debate about ordination. I am not pretending it does. A church still has to decide who stands in the pulpit and who governs, and that decision matters and cannot be dodged by spiritualizing it away. But it changes the spirit in which we hold the decision. If leadership is fundamentally a basin and a towel, then the highest ambition available to any Christian, man or woman, ordained or not, is already open to all of them, and no council can grant it or withhold it. The greatest in the kingdom is the servant of all, and that door has no gatekeeper.

## The verdict I will actually stand behind

So here is where I land, and I hold it against myself first. I want the women in my congregation to lead in every way my reading of Scripture permits, and my reading permits a great deal. But more than I want them to have the office, I want the whole church, myself at the front of the line, to stop treating leadership as a prize and start treating it as a cross. Because a church that gives women the pulpit and keeps the world's account of what a pulpit is for has not been reformed. It has only rearranged the seating. And a church that keeps women from the pulpit while its men grasp at authority like Gentile rulers has denied the very thing the office is supposed to embody.

The women were already leading in Acts. They were leading the way the kingdom leads, by serving, prophesying, hosting, funding, teaching, dying. The question was never really whether women could lead. The question is whether any of us, women or men, have understood what leading in this kingdom costs. The basin is still in the corner. It has been there the whole time. We keep stepping over it to argue about the pulpit.

chapters.title: Women and Mental Health: The Weight Nobody Sees
chapters.summary: The church has too often met a woman's suffering with a Bible verse and a suspicion. Scripture itself is more honest about the darkness than the sermons that quote it.
chapters.body:
Before I say anything else, I want to say the plain and necessary thing. What follows is a pastor thinking theologically about suffering. It is not medical advice, and it is not a substitute for a doctor, a therapist, or, if you are in danger tonight, the crisis line that exists precisely so that you do not have to be alone with the worst hour. If you are thinking of harming yourself, please reach out to a professional or call or text 988 in the United States. Theology and medicine are not rivals here. You need both, and this essay is only one of them.

Now the harder thing, the thing the church has too often gotten wrong, and that I have gotten wrong in rooms where a woman was quietly falling apart in front of me and I reached for a verse instead of a hand.

## The suffering that gets a suspicion instead of a hand

A woman came to me years ago and told me she thought she was losing her mind. She could not stop crying. She could not feel her children the way she used to. She woke at three in the morning with a dread she could not name. And she said, with a shame that has stayed with me, that she was afraid to tell anyone at church, because she knew what they would say. They would say she needed to trust God more. They would find the sin. They would hand her a verse about anxiety and joy and treat her collapse as a spiritual failure she could repent her way out of.

She was not wrong about what the church would say, because it is what the church often does say, and it is a specific cruelty. We meet a suffering we cannot see with a suspicion we should never have. When a woman breaks her arm, we do not ask what sin caused it. When a woman's mind is breaking, we too often do, and we dress the interrogation up as spiritual concern. I have watched women who were clinically ill be told they had a joy problem, a faith problem, a gratitude problem, when what they had was an illness, and the church made the illness lonelier than it already was.

> We would never tell a woman with a broken arm that she needed to trust God more. We say it constantly to the woman whose mind is broken, and we call the cruelty discernment.

## The Bible is more honest than the sermons

What makes this failure so galling is that the Bible itself is far more honest about the darkness than the people who quote it. The suspicion the church casts on the suffering woman cannot survive an actual reading of Scripture, because Scripture is full of the faithful in the pit.

Read the Psalms and count the ones that end in darkness. Psalm 88, the darkest of them all, ends without resolution: "You have caused my beloved and my friend to shun me; my companions have become darkness" (Psalm 88:18). That is the last verse. There is no upturn, no doxology, no light breaking. The Spirit of God inspired a prayer that ends in the dark and put it in the church's hymnbook, which means that a believer sitting in unrelieved darkness is not outside the faith. She is inside a psalm.

Elijah, days after the greatest victory of his ministry, collapses under a broom tree and asks God to let him die: "It is enough; now, O Lord, take away my life" (1 Kings 19:4). This is not a man in unbelief. This is the prophet who called down fire, and he is suicidal from exhaustion. And notice what God does not do. God does not rebuke him. God does not diagnose a sin. God lets him sleep, and sends an angel to feed him, and lets him sleep again, and feeds him again (1 Kings 19:5-7). The divine response to a servant's collapse is rest and food before it is a single word of theology. God treated the body first. The church that skips straight to the sermon is less patient with the broken than God was.

And there is a phrase in the New Testament we rush past. In Gethsemane, Jesus himself says, "My soul is very sorrowful, even to death" (Matthew 26:38). The Son of God, in his humanity, knew a sorrow that pressed to the edge of what a soul can bear. If sorrow to the point of death were evidence of faithlessness, it would convict our Lord. It does not. It sanctifies the darkness. It means the God we worship has been in the pit and did not consider it beneath his dignity to feel it.

## The weight that is specifically hers

There is a further honesty owed here, which is that women carry weights that men structurally do not, and the church has been slow to reckon with them.

There is the biological weight. The hormonal upheavals of the female body, in the postpartum months, in the long grind of the reproductive years, in the changes of midlife, are real physiological events with real effects on the mind, and treating them as moral events is a category error that harms women. Postpartum depression is not a failure of maternal love. It is an illness with a physical mechanism, and a woman drowning in it needs a physician and a community, not a lecture on gratitude for the child she is too ill to enjoy. When we spiritualize what is biological, we heap shame on a woman who is already suffering, and shame is fuel to the fire we are pretending to put out.

There is the weight of the unseen labor, the invisible cognitive load of running a household, the mental ledger of everyone's needs that so often falls to women and is never counted as work because it produces nothing you can point to. A woman can be exhausted to the bone by a labor that leaves no visible product, and be told she did nothing all day, and begin to believe it. That is a specific erosion, and it wears on the mind in ways the culture and the church have only recently begun to name.

And there is the weight of being the one who holds everyone else together. In many families it is the woman who monitors the emotional temperature of the whole household, who absorbs the moods, who manages the peace. That role is real work and it is depleting, and the person doing it is often the last one anyone thinks to check on, because her whole function is to be the one who is fine so that everyone else can fall apart on her. When she finally cannot hold it anymore, the system that depended on her holding it has no idea what to do.

## What the church owes and has often withheld

So what should we have done, and what should we do now? I want to be concrete without pretending there is a four-step fix, because there is not, and anyone who offers you one for the suffering mind is selling something.

We owe the suffering woman the same thing God gave Elijah under the broom tree: rest, food, presence, and time before a single word of correction. We owe her the refusal to diagnose her illness as sin. We owe her a theology robust enough to hold Psalm 88, a faith that does not require her to fake the doxology she cannot feel. We owe her the full use of God's common grace, which includes the physician and the counselor and the medication that, for many, is not a failure of faith but a mercy of God delivered through the ordinary means of medicine, the same way an antibiotic is. The God who made the body made the ways the body is healed, and there is no more shame in a prescription for the mind than in one for the blood.

And we owe her the truth that her worth does not rise and fall with her ability to function. This is the deepest thing, and it is where the gospel actually bites. A woman whose whole life has been justified by what she produces, the clean house, the fed family, the held-together everyone, will experience her collapse as the collapse of her worth, because her worth was built on her output. The gospel says her worth was never her output. She is loved by God for reasons that have nothing to do with whether she got out of bed today, purchased at the cross, secured before she did anything and safe even now when she can do nothing. On her worst day, flattened and useless by every measure the world uses, she is worth exactly what she was worth on her best, because the price was set by Christ and not by her. That is not a verse to hand her and walk away. It is a truth to sit inside with her, for as long as it takes, in the dark, the way God sat with Elijah and the way Christ sweated in the garden.

## Where the culture gets it half right

I want to test the secular account at its strongest, because the church's instinct to dismiss it wholesale is part of what made us useless to suffering women in the first place. The wider culture now speaks openly about mental health, has torn down some of the stigma, and has insisted that depression and anxiety are real conditions and not moral failures. On all of that, the culture is right, and it is right against a church that was often wrong, and honesty requires me to say so plainly.

The research the culture draws on is not fluff. The World Health Organization has documented for years that women are diagnosed with depression at roughly twice the rate of men, a disparity that holds across cultures and cannot be explained away as mere reporting bias. Whatever the tangled causes, biological, social, and circumstantial, the weight really does fall harder on women, and a church that will not say so is refusing to see what is in front of it. The secular world saw it first, named it, and stopped shaming the sufferer, and every one of those was a mercy the church should have offered and did not.

But the secular account, strong as it is on the symptom, tends to be thin on the anthropology, and this is where Scripture goes deeper rather than merely disagreeing. The culture can tell a woman her depression is not her fault. It struggles to tell her why she matters when she cannot function, because it has largely located human worth in autonomy, productivity, and self-actualization, the very things depression strips away. A therapeutic culture that grounds a person's value in her flourishing has nothing to say to the person who cannot flourish, and so it can remove the shame of the illness without answering the deeper terror underneath it, which is the fear that a self that produces nothing is a self worth nothing. Only a gospel that grounds worth outside the self, in the love and the purchase of God, can reach that terror. The culture got the symptom right and the anthropology incomplete. The church should have offered both and for too long offered neither.

## The weight this leaves

The woman who came to me afraid to tell anyone got help, real help, medical and communal and slow. She is well now, mostly, in the way that people who have been to the bottom are well, which is to say she carries the memory of it and it has made her gentler with everyone else who goes there. But I think often of the fear she named, the certainty that the church would find the sin. She was not paranoid. She had watched us do it to others. We had trained her to expect a suspicion in the place where she should have found a shelter.

I think often, too, about how much of what I mistook for a spiritual condition was simply a body that had run out of what it needed to keep going. The line between the soul and the body is far thinner than my early theology allowed. When Elijah wanted to die, God did not begin with his theology; God began with sleep and bread, because sometimes the most spiritual thing a crushed person needs is rest and food and a doctor, and the reordering of the heart comes after the body has been given a chance to recover. A pastor who cannot tell the difference between a sin to be confessed and an illness to be treated will wound the very people he most wants to help, and I have been that pastor, reaching for repentance where I should have reached for a physician's number and a warm meal and a promise to stay.

That is the failure I cannot argue my way around. The Bible we hold gives us Psalm 88 and Elijah under the tree and Christ in Gethsemane, a whole scriptural vocabulary for the faithful in the dark, and we set it aside to interrogate the suffering. The weight nobody sees is heavy enough. The church was never supposed to add to it. Too often it has, and I among them. The verse I should have led with, every time, was not the one about anxiety. It was the one that says he is near to the brokenhearted, and saves the crushed in spirit (Psalm 34:18). Near. Not diagnosing from across the room. Near.

chapters.title: Women and Work: Calling Beyond the Home Debate
chapters.summary: The evangelical fight over whether women should work has argued for decades on a battlefield the Bible never chose. There is an older and larger question underneath it.
chapters.body:
I came to faith as an adult, out of atheism, and one of the strange things about arriving late to the church is that you can still see its arguments from the outside before you learn to feel them from the inside. The first evangelical fight I stumbled into was the one about women and work. Should Christian women have careers? Should mothers stay home? I remember thinking, with the flat literalism of a new reader, that I could not find the debate in the Bible I was reading. I found something larger and stranger, and it did not fit either side.

Two decades later I have five sons and a working understanding of how much labor a household actually requires, and I am more convinced than ever that the standard evangelical argument about women and work is fought on a field the Scriptures never chose. Both sides have accepted a framing that would have baffled the people who wrote the book we all claim to obey.

## The field nobody chose

The framing is this: there is the home, and there is work, and they are two places, and the question is which one a woman belongs in. That framing feels ancient and biblical. It is neither. It is roughly a hundred and eighty years old, and it is a product of the Industrial Revolution.

Before the factory, the home and the workplace were the same building. The household was the unit of production. A farm, a shop, a trade, a bakery, a weaving business, all of it happened where the family lived, and everyone in the family labored, including the wife, including the children, including the servants and apprentices. The Greek word for household, *oikos*, is the root of our word economy, and that is not a coincidence. The household *was* the economy. The idea that a man goes away to a place called work while a woman stays in a place called home would have been unintelligible to Abraham, to Boaz, to Priscilla, to almost everyone in Scripture.

What separated the two was the factory. When production moved out of the home and into the mill, men followed the paying labor out the door, and the home was left as a place of consumption and childrearing rather than production. Only then did a new ideology arise to explain the arrangement, what historians call the doctrine of separate spheres, the belief that the man's proper realm is the harsh public world of commerce and the woman's is the tender private world of the domestic hearth. The historian Barbara Welter named a related nineteenth-century ideal the Cult of True Womanhood in a landmark 1966 essay, and its four cardinal virtues were piety, purity, submissiveness, and domesticity. That fourth one, domesticity, is the one the church baptized. We took a Victorian economic accident and called it the created order.

## What Proverbs 31 actually describes

Nothing exposes this more sharply than the passage most often preached to keep women at home. Proverbs 31. The excellent wife. If you have only heard it read at Mother's Day, you have heard it sentimentally, and you have almost certainly missed what she does with her days.

She evaluates a field and buys it (Proverbs 31:16). She plants a vineyard from her own earnings. She "perceives that her merchandise is profitable" (31:18), which means she is running a business with a margin. She makes linen garments and sells them, and delivers sashes to the merchant (31:24). She is a manufacturer with a distribution channel. "She considers a field and buys it; with the fruit of her hands she plants a vineyard." The verbs are commercial. She is trading, negotiating, producing, and profiting, and the text holds all of this up not as scandalous but as the very definition of the woman "who fears the Lord" (31:30).

The passage does not describe a woman confined to a private sphere. It describes a woman whose economic activity extends into the marketplace as a matter of course, because in the ancient world there was no wall between her household and the economy. She is praised in the gates, the place of public commerce and civic life. The chapter we cite to send women home is a chapter about a woman running an enterprise.

> We turned a Victorian factory arrangement into a doctrine and then found a Hebrew businesswoman inconvenient. So we read her sentimentally, which is a polite way of not reading her at all.

## The word the whole thing turns on

Underneath the work debate is a bigger idea, and if you get the bigger idea the smaller debate mostly dissolves. The idea is vocation.

Vocation comes from the Latin *vocare*, to call, and it was one of the recoveries of the Reformation. Before the sixteenth century, the language of calling was reserved for the clergy and the religious orders. You had a vocation if you were a priest, a monk, a nun. Everyone else just had a job, spiritually second-class labor performed while the truly called people prayed. Martin Luther detonated that in the 1520s. In his treatise on the estate of marriage and throughout his writing on the priesthood of all believers, Luther argued that the milkmaid and the magistrate and the mother have callings as holy as the monk, that God milks the cows through the milkmaid, that the humblest domestic labor done in faith is worship. The word for calling, in German *Beruf*, comes to mean both the divine summons and one's ordinary occupation. Those two meanings fused in the Reformation and have never fully come apart.

Now hold that recovery against the work debate, and watch what happens. If vocation is the summons of God to serve your neighbor through your labor, then the question is never whether a woman should work. All labor that serves a neighbor in faith is a calling, whether it happens over a keyboard or a cradle. The mother teaching a two-year-old to speak is doing holy work. The physician setting a broken arm is doing holy work. The single woman running an accounting firm is doing holy work. None of these is a fallback from the others. Each is a place where God is at work through a human being for the sake of other human beings.

## Where the harder truth lives

I do not want to make this too clean, because clean is usually a sign that I have stopped telling the truth. There are real tensions here that the vocation framework does not dissolve, and pretending otherwise would be a kind of lie.

The first is that children are not a job you can do in your spare hours, and someone has to do it. In our house, with five sons, the sheer volume of formation required, the meals and the reading and the discipline and the presence, is not a hobby squeezed around careers. It is a vocation in the fullest Reformation sense, and it is enormous, and it usually falls disproportionately on my wife in ways that our theology of vocation honors and our economy of vocation does not pay for. To say a mother's work is holy and then to structure a household as if it were free is a contradiction I have lived and not resolved. The dignity we assign in the sermon has to show up in the division of labor at home, or the sermon is a decoration.

The second tension is that work under the fall is not pure calling. Genesis 3 promises that the ground will bring forth thorns and that labor will come with sweat (Genesis 3:17-19), and that curse falls on the woman's work as well as the man's. A great deal of what women do for pay is exhausting, underpaid, and unseen, and a theology that only celebrates work as fulfillment has not read past Genesis 3. Sometimes work is just the thorns. A robust doctrine of vocation has to hold both, the dignity of the calling and the groaning of the cursed ground, without collapsing into either the prosperity gospel of the fulfilled career or the false piety that treats all ambition as pride.

## The women the New Testament put to work

If the separate-spheres ideology were the created order, the early church did not get the memo, and the evidence is embarrassing to anyone who wants to keep women out of visible labor in the kingdom. Read the sixteenth chapter of Romans, where Paul greets the people he is relying on, and count the women. He commends Phoebe, a deacon of the church at Cenchreae, and calls her a patron, the Greek *prostatis*, a word for a benefactor with the means to support others (Romans 16:1-2). He greets Prisca, whom he names before her husband Aquila, a couple who "risked their necks for my life" and who had earlier taken the eloquent Apollos aside and taught him the way of God more accurately (Acts 18:26). He greets Mary, who "worked hard" for the church, and Tryphaena and Tryphosa, "workers in the Lord," and Persis, "who has worked hard in the Lord" (Romans 16:6, 12). The verb for hard labor, *kopiao*, is the same one Paul uses for his own exhausting apostolic work.

These were not women confined to a private hearth doing invisible domestic tasks. They were financing the mission, hosting the church in their homes, teaching, traveling, and laboring in ways the church visibly depended on. Lydia, the first convert in Europe, was a dealer in purple cloth, a businesswoman running a trade in luxury goods, and the church at Philippi met in her house (Acts 16:14-15). The early Christian movement, born into a Roman world with its own rigid ideas about a woman's place, kept putting women to work in the most consequential labor there was. The Victorian doctrine that a woman's calling ends at her front door cannot survive a single reading of Romans 16.

I raise this not to settle every question about office and authority, which is a separate matter that faithful churches dispute, but to make a narrower and undeniable point. The reflex that treats a woman's work outside the home as a concession to modernity, a departure from the biblical pattern, has the history exactly backward. The biblical pattern is a church staffed and funded and advanced by women who worked hard in the Lord, and Paul knew their names and wrote them down so we would too.

## The verdict the debate was hiding

So I want to end by naming what I think the home-versus-work debate was actually protecting, because it was protecting something real, and I do not want to be glib about people who felt they were defending the family.

What it was protecting was the conviction that children matter, that formation is not automatic, that a household is a garden that dies untended, and that a culture which treats childrearing as an obstacle to real life has lost its mind. That conviction is right. The church that fought for it was fighting for something worth fighting for. It just chose the wrong hill. It defended the family by defending a Victorian floor plan, and in doing so it told half the church that their labor in the marketplace was a compromise and the other half that their labor at home was invisible. Both of those messages were false, and both of them wounded women I have pastored.

I have watched women wounded by both halves of this. I have watched a gifted woman apologize for her ambition as though the drive to build something good were a character flaw peculiar to women who would not stay in their lane. And I have watched a mother, worn to nothing by the unpaid and unending labor of forming small souls, absorb the message that she had opted out of anything that counted, that the real action was happening in offices she had left. I have watched the same woman, years later, told by a different corner of the church that she had betrayed her home the moment she took a paying job to keep the lights on. She could not win, because the game was rigged from the start against the possibility that her labor, wherever it happened, was simply good. Both women were lied to. Both were doing holy work. The lie in each case was the same lie wearing opposite clothes: that there is a hierarchy of callings with a woman's true place fixed somewhere on it, and that her worth is a matter of standing in the right spot. There is no such hierarchy. There is only the summons, and the faith with which she answers it.

The truth underneath is older and harder and better. Every woman is called. The mother and the merchant, the teacher and the trader, the one raising sons and the one running a firm and the many doing both at once, are all standing in the same place, the place where God works through human hands for the sake of a neighbor. The question was never whether a woman should work. The question is the one the whole Bible asks of everyone: what has God called you to, and are you doing it in faith? That question does not sort women into spheres. It summons them. And a summons is a heavier and more honorable thing than a place to belong.

chapters.title: Women in Church History: The Voices They Silenced
chapters.summary: Perpetua faced the arena. Macrina taught the theologians. Julian saw visions in a plague year. Catherine rebuked a pope. The church has always had women it later tried to forget.
chapters.body:
When I first read church history seriously, I read it as a chain of men. Athanasius, Augustine, Anselm, Aquinas, Luther, Calvin, Wesley, Edwards. It is a real chain and I owe those men a debt I cannot pay. But I read it that way partly because that is how it was handed to me, and the handing had edited out a whole set of names that were there the entire time, doing theology, facing death, rebuking the powerful. I want to walk you through six of them, in order, across sixteen centuries, because the argument that women were absent from the serious life of the church is not an argument the historical record can bear.

## Perpetua, the arena, 203

We have her diary. That is the astonishing thing. The Passion of Perpetua and Felicity contains what scholars regard as one of the earliest surviving texts written by a Christian woman in her own voice. Vibia Perpetua was a young mother in Carthage, around twenty-two years old, nursing an infant, when she was arrested during the persecution under the emperor Septimius Severus in the year 203.

Her father comes to the prison and begs her to recant, to think of the child, to save herself. It is one of the most human scenes in early Christian literature. She loves him and she will not move. She points to a small water pot and asks him whether it can be called by any name other than what it is. No, he says. "Neither can I call myself anything other than what I am, a Christian," she answers. She records her own visions in the days before her death. She writes as a theologian and a mother and a woman about to die, and she does not flinch. When they lead her into the arena to be gored by a wild heifer and then finished by the sword, the account tells us the young gladiator's hand trembled, and she guided the blade to her own throat. The church remembered her name for centuries. Somewhere along the way many of us stopped hearing it.

I want to sit with one detail, because it undoes a lazy assumption. Perpetua was not a poor and desperate woman with nothing to lose. The text describes her as well born and liberally educated, honorably married, with an infant at the breast. She had every earthly reason to recant, a family that loved her, a child that needed her, a social position that made her death a scandal and a waste in the eyes of everyone watching. And she was, by the account we have, the leader of the group of martyrs, the one whose visions guided them, the one whose calm steadied the others. In the third century, when a woman's public voice was heavily constrained, the church preserved and treasured a document in which a young mother is the theological and spiritual authority over a group of men and women facing death together. That the early church chose to keep her diary, to read it aloud in worship on the anniversary of her death for generations, tells you what that church valued and what a later church quietly declined to pass on.

## Macrina, who taught the teachers, fourth century

You know the Cappadocian Fathers, Basil the Great and Gregory of Nyssa and Gregory of Nazianzus, architects of the doctrine of the Trinity that the whole church would confess at Constantinople in 381. What you may not know is that Basil and Gregory of Nyssa had an older sister, Macrina, and that Gregory himself wrote a treatise crediting her as his teacher.

He titled the work On the Soul and the Resurrection, and in it he casts Macrina as "the Teacher," the one instructing him in the deepest questions of the faith as she lay dying. He modeled the dialogue on Plato's account of Socrates' death, casting his own sister in the Socratic role, the sage guiding the student through the last things. Gregory of Nyssa, one of the greatest theological minds the church has produced, sat at the feet of his sister and said so in writing. He also wrote her biography, the Life of Macrina, an act of open reverence for a woman he considered his intellectual and spiritual superior. The tradition kept his theology and quietly lost his teacher.

## Julian of Norwich, the plague year, 1373

In May of 1373, in the city of Norwich in England, a woman we know only as Julian, named for the church she was later attached to, fell gravely ill and received a series of sixteen visions, what she called showings. She recovered and spent the rest of her long life, as an anchoress walled into a cell beside a church, meditating on what she had seen. She wrote the visions down in a work called Revelations of Divine Love, which holds the distinction of being the earliest surviving book written in English by a woman.

She lived through the era of the Black Death, which killed perhaps a third of Europe, and she wrote not sentimental comfort but hard-won hope. Her most famous line comes from a vision in which she held a small thing the size of a hazelnut in her hand and understood it to be all that is made, fragile, and yet sustained because "God loves it." And her most quoted words, spoken in the visions in the voice of Christ, are these: "All shall be well, and all shall be well, and all manner of thing shall be well." That is not the sentence of a woman who has not seen suffering. That is the sentence of a woman who has seen a third of her world die and refused to let go of the love beneath the terror. I did not learn her name in seminary. I learned it later, alone, and I was poorer for the delay.

She did something else, too, that deserves mention, because it shows a theological mind at work and not merely a devotional one. Julian meditated at length on the motherhood of God, on the ways Scripture itself uses maternal images for God, the God who says through Isaiah, "As one whom his mother comforts, so I will comfort you" (Isaiah 66:13), the Christ who longed to gather Jerusalem "as a hen gathers her brood under her wings" (Matthew 23:37). She did not invent these images. She drew them out of the text and pressed on them with a seriousness the tradition around her had not, writing of Christ as our mother who feeds us with himself. This is not sentiment. It is careful biblical reflection on a strand of Scripture the church had underused, done by a woman walled into a cell beside a church during a plague, and it has fed serious theologians ever since. The idea that the female contemplatives were merely emotional while the men did the rigorous work does not survive an honest reading of what Julian actually wrote.

## Catherine of Siena, who rebuked a pope, fourteenth century

Catherine was born in Siena in 1347, the year the plague reached Italy. She was the twenty-third or twenty-fourth child of a dyer, unlettered as a girl, and she became one of the most consequential figures of the fourteenth century. She dictated hundreds of letters and a major work of mysticism, The Dialogue, and she did something almost no one in her age would have dared. She wrote to Pope Gregory XI, then living in Avignon in France rather than in Rome, and told him to go home.

Her letters to the pope are not deferential. They are urgent, blunt, and pastoral in the prophetic sense, addressing him as "babbo," father, and then telling him plainly to be a man and return the papacy to Rome and reform the corruption of the church. And he went. The return of the papacy to Rome in 1377 is bound up with her advocacy. A woman with no formal education, no office, no title, moved the most powerful man in Western Christendom by the sheer force of her conviction that the church had lost its nerve. In 1970 the Roman Catholic Church named her a Doctor of the Church, one of only a handful of women given that honor. The Protestant world that formed me barely mentioned her at all.

## Teresa of Avila, who reformed an order, sixteenth century

Teresa of Avila lived from 1515 to 1582, a Spanish Carmelite nun who reformed her religious order, founded new communities against fierce opposition, and wrote works of spiritual theology, The Interior Castle and her autobiography, that have never gone out of print. She wrote under the shadow of the Spanish Inquisition, as a woman of partly Jewish descent, in an environment where a woman claiming direct spiritual experience risked being investigated for heresy. She wrote anyway, with wit and steel.

Her account of the soul as an interior castle with many rooms, through which one moves toward union with God at the center, is one of the enduring achievements of Christian spiritual writing. Like Catherine, she was later named a Doctor of the Church, in 1970. She was a mystic who was also a formidable administrator, and she gave the lie to the idea that contemplation and competence cannot live in the same woman.

## Phoebe Palmer, who lit a revival, nineteenth century

Closer to my own tradition, Phoebe Palmer lived from 1807 to 1874, a Methodist laywoman in New York whose Tuesday Meetings for the Promotion of Holiness became an engine of the nineteenth-century Holiness movement, which shaped American evangelicalism in ways we still feel. She was a theologian of Christian sanctification, a revivalist who preached to thousands, and in 1859 she published The Promise of the Father, a defense of women's right to preach and testify, arguing from the prophecy of Joel that Peter quotes at Pentecost: "your sons and your daughters shall prophesy" (Acts 2:17).

She was not asking for a theory. She was defending what the Spirit was already doing through women in the revivals of her day. And the movement she helped shape is one of the streams that flows down into the church I now pastor.

It is worth pausing on the pattern that runs through the whole century after her. The nineteenth-century revivals and the missionary and abolitionist movements they fueled were disproportionately driven by women, and the historians of American religion, Mark Noll and Nathan Hatch among them, have documented how the democratizing energy of that era opened doors for women to preach, testify, teach, and organize on a scale the established churches had not permitted. The temperance movement, the earliest campaigns against slavery, the founding of missions and schools and homes for the destitute, were staffed and often led by women who understood their faith to demand it. When you strip these women out of the story, as the tidy male chain of theologians does, you do not just lose a few names. You lose the actual engine of much of the practical Christianity of the age.

## What the pattern says

I could have named more, and the fact that I had to choose is itself part of the argument. I passed over Hildegard of Bingen, the twelfth-century abbess who composed music still performed today, wrote works of medicine and theology, and corresponded with popes and emperors as an equal. I passed over Katharina von Bora, who fled a convent, married Martin Luther, and ran the household and finances that made his reforming work possible, a woman Luther himself called his lord and often deferred to. I passed over Susanna Wesley, who taught and shaped the two sons, John and Charles, who would ignite a movement, doing her theological formation of them at a kitchen table with nineteen children and a mostly absent husband. The list of the omitted is longer than the list I included. That is not because the women were rare. It is because they were many, and I had space for six.

## Why the editing happened, named honestly

It would be easy to blame a conspiracy, and there was none. What there was is something more ordinary and harder to fix. History gets written by those with access to writing, and for most of the church's life that access was controlled by men, in monasteries and universities and the clergy, so the histories they wrote naturally centered the men they knew and the offices they held. A woman's influence, exercised often through counsel, hospitality, patronage, teaching of children, and personal holiness rather than through titled office, left fewer official traces and so slipped more easily out of the record. The bias was not always a decision to silence. It was frequently just the shape of who held the pen. But the effect on those of us who inherited the edited record is the same whether the cause was malice or mere convenience. We received a church that looked more male than it was, and we passed the distortion on without checking it.

Six women, from 203 to the nineteenth century. A martyr, a teacher of theologians, a mystic in a plague, a woman who moved a pope, a reformer of an order, a revivalist. This is not a list of exceptions God grudgingly permitted. This is a continuous line running the entire length of church history, and if you have never heard most of these names, the question worth asking is not why the church lacked women of depth. The church did not lack them. The question is who decided which names to pass down, and why the ones passed down skewed so heavily male.

I have to answer that question with myself in the frame, because I have been one of the people passing the tradition down. Every reading list I have handed a young Christian, every history I have taught, has been a set of choices about who gets remembered. For years my choices reproduced the silence I now grieve. I did not silence Perpetua. She said her piece in an arena in 203 and it survives to this day. But I kept my mouth shut about her, which in the economy of memory amounts to a quieter version of the same thing.

The voices were never actually silenced. They were recorded, written down, preserved by the very church that later stopped repeating them. That is the strange mercy of it. They are still on the shelf. Perpetua is still guiding the trembling blade. Macrina is still teaching her brother as she dies. Catherine is still telling the pope to be a man. All that is required to end the silence is for someone to read the names out loud. I have been slow to do it. I am doing it now, and I am aware that I should have started sooner.

chapters.title: Women in the Bible They Don't Teach You About
chapters.summary: Deborah judged Israel. Huldah authenticated Scripture. Junia was called an apostle. The Bible is fuller of women with authority than the sermons I grew up on ever let on.
chapters.body:
I came to faith late, and I came to it suspicious. When you arrive at Christianity from atheism, you do not arrive with the assumptions a churched child carries. You arrive with a list of accusations, and near the top of my list was this one: the Bible erases women. I had heard that outside the church, and then I walked inside the church and heard it confirmed by omission. The women I met in sermons were quiet, supportive, and safely offstage. Sarah laughed. Ruth gleaned. Mary treasured things in her heart. I was not told there were women who commanded armies and authenticated Scripture, and I want to know why I was not told.

So let me tell you what I found when I finally read the text instead of the paraphrase of the text I had been handed.

I should say at the outset why this matters to me beyond the intellectual accusation. I have five sons and no daughters, which means I have spent two decades thinking about how a man forms boys. But I pastor a church full of daughters, and I was raised by a woman who held a household together alone because my father was not there to help her do it. The women who kept me alive as a boy were not offstage in my life. They were the whole stage. When I opened the Bible expecting them to be absent and found them everywhere, something in me that had been braced for disappointment relaxed, and then something else in me got angry, because I understood how much had been kept from me and from everyone in the pews beside me.

## Deborah, who was already leading before the men agreed to it

Judges 4 does not soften what it says. "Now Deborah, a prophetess, the wife of Lappidoth, was judging Israel at that time" (Judges 4:4). The Hebrew verb there, shaphat, is the same verb used of Gideon, of Samson, of every judge God raised up in that book. She is not filling in. She is not a placeholder until a real leader shows up. She holds court under a palm tree and Israel comes to her for judgment, which in that era meant she carried both civil and spiritual authority for a nation.

Barak, the general, will not go to war unless she comes with him. Read that slowly. The military commander of Israel refuses to move without the woman prophet at his side. And Deborah tells him plainly that because he insisted on her presence, the glory of the victory will go to a woman, and it does, to Jael with a tent peg (Judges 4:9). The book of Judges is a book about the failure of leadership in Israel, one long descent, and sitting near the top of that descent as one of its bright moments is a woman.

I was taught that Deborah was an exception God permitted because no man would step up. I have heard pastors say it from the pulpit as though it were in the text. It is not in the text. The text does not apologize for her. The text does not explain her away. We do that. The apology is ours, not God's.

And there is more. The victory song in Judges 5, which scholars regard as one of the oldest passages in the entire Hebrew Bible, some dating its composition to within a century or two of the events it describes, is attributed to Deborah herself. "Then sang Deborah and Barak the son of Abinoam on that day" (Judges 5:1). She is credited as a poet and a theologian of Israel's history, composing the sacred song that interprets what God has done. In that song she names herself: "until I arose, I, Deborah, arose as a mother in Israel" (Judges 5:7). A mother in Israel, and also its judge, its prophet, and the author of one of its oldest hymns. The categories we like to keep separate, the maternal and the authoritative, she held together in a single breath, and the text celebrates the union rather than straining at it.

## Huldah, who told the king whether the Bible was real

In 622 B.C., during the reign of Josiah, a scroll was found during the temple renovation. Second Kings 22 tells the story. The scroll appears to be a portion of Deuteronomy, and it terrifies the king because it names judgments Judah has been ignoring for generations. Josiah needs to know if the scroll is authentic, if it truly speaks for God. He sends the high priest Hilkiah and the royal officials to find out.

They do not go to Jeremiah, who was prophesying at that time. They do not go to Zephaniah. They go to Huldah, a prophetess living in Jerusalem (2 Kings 22:14). And Huldah renders the verdict. She authenticates the word of God for the king of Judah. "Thus says the LORD, the God of Israel" (2 Kings 22:15), she begins, and the reform of Josiah, one of the great revivals in the Old Testament, proceeds on the authority of her judgment about what counted as Scripture.

Think about what that means. At a hinge moment in the formation of the canon, the question of whether a text was truly the word of God was answered by a woman, and the priests and the king accepted her answer without recorded objection. I went thirty years without hearing her name. That is not the Bible's failure. That is a failure downstream of it, and I have participated in it.

## Junia, the apostle they turned into a man

Romans 16 is Paul's long list of greetings, and it is full of women doing real work. In verse 7 Paul writes, "Greet Andronicus and Junia, my kinsmen and my fellow prisoners. They are well known to the apostles, and they were in Christ before me." Junia is a woman's name. It was a common Roman woman's name. And Paul calls her, along with Andronicus, "well known to the apostles," or as many scholars render the Greek, "well known among the apostles," which would make her an apostle herself.

John Chrysostom, preaching in the fourth century, took it plainly. "Oh how great is the devotion of this woman," he said, "that she should be even counted worthy of the appellation of apostle." He did not blink at a female apostle. The blinking came later. Sometime in the medieval period the name was quietly altered in some manuscripts and translations to Junias, a masculine form, a name for which we have no attestation anywhere in the ancient world. The scholar Eldon Jay Epp documented this in his 2005 study, tracing how a woman named Junia became a man named Junias in the printed Greek New Testament for much of the twentieth century, until the textual evidence forced the correction back.

We changed her name. Not God. We did. Faced with a woman the text called an apostle, translators found it easier to change the woman than to change their assumptions. I want to sit in that discomfort rather than rush past it.

I want to be fair to the other reading, because honesty demands it. Some scholars argue that the Greek phrase means Junia was well known to the apostles rather than counted among them, which would make her esteemed by the apostles without holding the office herself. That is a legitimate grammatical possibility and I will not pretend the case is closed. But notice that even the more modest reading leaves us with a woman whom Paul names alongside her husband, calls his kinsman and fellow prisoner, and says was in Christ before he was, a woman esteemed by the apostolic circle and imprisoned for the faith. Whichever way the grammar finally falls, the attempt to erase her by turning her into a man named Junias was not a grammatical decision. It was a decision made in advance about what a woman was permitted to be, and then imposed on the text. That is the part I cannot excuse, and the part I recognize in myself, because I have read my own assumptions back into Scripture more times than I have caught myself doing it.

## Phoebe, who carried the letter

Romans opens the sixteenth chapter this way: "I commend to you our sister Phoebe, a servant of the church at Cenchreae" (Romans 16:1). The word translated servant is diakonos, deacon, the same word Paul uses of himself and of Timothy. He continues, "that you may help her in whatever she may need from you, for she has been a patron of many and of myself as well" (Romans 16:2). The word patron there, prostatis, carries the sense of a benefactor, a protector, one who stands before others on their behalf.

Phoebe was almost certainly the person who carried the letter to the Romans from Corinth to Rome. That is a staggering thing to consider. The most theologically dense letter in the New Testament, the document that lit the fuse under Augustine and Luther and Wesley, was entrusted to a woman to deliver, and as the courier she would have been the one to read it aloud and answer the first questions the Roman church had about it. The first interpreter of Romans was Phoebe. I was not taught that either.

## Priscilla, who taught the great preacher

Acts 18 introduces Priscilla and her husband Aquila, tentmakers who work alongside Paul. When the eloquent preacher Apollos comes to Ephesus preaching accurately but incompletely, it is Priscilla and Aquila who "took him aside and explained to him the way of God more accurately" (Acts 18:26). Notice the order. Luke names Priscilla first in that verse, and in most of the places the couple appears, her name comes first, which in the ancient convention often signaled prominence. A woman helped correct and complete the theology of one of the early church's most gifted preachers.

Think about what a strange sentence that is for those who insist a woman may never instruct a man in matters of doctrine. Here is a man, Apollos, described as eloquent and "competent in the Scriptures" (Acts 18:24), being taken aside and taught the way of God more accurately by a married couple in which Luke, contrary to his culture's convention, names the wife first. The verb Luke uses is not a soft word for suggestion. They explained, they set forth, they instructed. And the New Testament records it without a hint of apology or qualification, as simply what happened, the way the truth got to Apollos so that he could go on to be a powerful help to the believers in Achaia. The church that produced the New Testament did not seem to find Priscilla's teaching of Apollos remarkable enough to comment on. The later church found it remarkable enough to explain away. The distance between those two reactions is the distance I am trying to name in this whole essay.

## The daughters of Zelophehad, who changed the law

In Numbers 27 five sisters, Mahlah, Noah, Hoglah, Milcah, and Tirzah, come before Moses and the whole assembly. Their father has died without sons, and under the existing law his inheritance and name would vanish. They argue their case. "Why should the name of our father be taken away from his clan because he had no son? Give to us a possession among our father's brothers" (Numbers 27:4). And here is the sentence I cannot get past: Moses brings their case before the LORD, and the LORD says, "The daughters of Zelophehad are right" (Numbers 27:7). God amends the inheritance law of Israel because five women stood up and said the law as it stood was unjust to them. Their appeal did not merely get an exception. It changed the statute for everyone after them.

## Mary Magdalene, the apostle to the apostles

All four Gospels place women at the empty tomb first. In John 20, Mary Magdalene meets the risen Christ, mistakes him for the gardener, and then hears him speak her name. He gives her the commission: "go to my brothers and say to them, I am ascending to my Father and your Father, to my God and your God" (John 20:17). She goes and announces to the disciples, "I have seen the Lord" (John 20:18).

The first witness of the resurrection, the first evangelist of the risen Christ, the first person commissioned to carry the news on which all of Christianity stands, was a woman. The medieval church called her apostola apostolorum, the apostle to the apostles, and they were right to. In a culture where a woman's testimony was not admissible in a court of law, God chose women as the first witnesses of the central event of history. If the early church had invented the resurrection story, as skeptics like me once assumed, they would never have staked it on witnesses no court would believe. The women at the tomb are, oddly, one of the strongest arguments for the thing actually happening.

## So why the silence

I do not want to overstate my case, and I will not pretend the Bible reads like a modern manifesto. It was written into patriarchal worlds and it names those worlds honestly, including their cruelty to women. But the honest reader has to reckon with how much more the text contains than the tradition passed down. The erasure I once blamed on the Bible was, I discovered, largely an erasure performed by its readers. We inherited a curated Bible. Someone chose which women to preach and which to skip, and the ones they skipped were often the ones with authority.

I say we, and I mean it. I have preached forty sermons on David and Paul before I ever preached one on Deborah or Huldah. That was a choice, and it was mine, and it taught a room full of daughters that Scripture had little for them but a supporting role. It was not the text that taught them that. It was me.

The women are in the book. They were always in the book. The question is whether we have the courage to preach the book we actually have instead of the one we were handed. Deborah is still sitting under her palm tree. Huldah is still holding the scroll. Mary is still running from the tomb with the only news that finally matters. They have been there the whole time. We are the ones who looked away.
